clue.text: Skier perhaps embraced by Miss World

indicators.note: to be embraced is to be held in someone's arms, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: a miss is a young woman, a gal
a skier is a ball hit high into the air, as a lob is; 'perhaps' marks the example

explanation.surface: A ski champion is hugged by the newly crowned Miss World.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss World' reads as one title, but it splits: 'Miss' is the outer piece and 'World' the definition. In cricket a skier is a mis-hit that goes straight up.
explanation.definitionFit: Something world-wide in scope, such as a world crisis, can be called a global crisis.

blocks.note: first meaning: pale in colour, as fair hair or skin
second meaning: something that sheds ... on a problem, a hint

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two meanings; crossword solvers also call each grid entry a light, which gives the clue a knowing wink.
explanation.definitionFit: Pale colouring is described as light, and a hint that illuminates a mystery throws light on it.

clue.text: Microscopic organism or suchlike arising in metal

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
the little phrase is placed inside the other word

blocks.note: etc, short for et cetera, means 'and so on' or 'or suchlike'
barium is a metallic element

explanation.surface: A tiny organism, or something like it, is found growing in a piece of metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bacterium is a single-celled germ, visible only under a microscope.

clue.text: Leader in love with gold carriage

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: first letter of love
'and' means together with
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A leading figure, in love, arrives with a golden carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A landau is a four-wheeled horse-drawn coach with a folding top.

indicators.note: being beyond something means coming after it, which fixes the order of the two parts

blocks.note: he's, short for 'he is', in the possessive-looking form
Peru is a South American country; Peru's keeps the 's

explanation.surface: Someone's country lies far beyond another man's planet.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 's endings are read as 'is': he's and Peru's, with the country placed after the man.
explanation.definitionFit: Hesperus is the evening star, the planet Venus seen in the west after sunset.

clue.text: So here honest criminal has concealed publication in drawer

indicators.note: something criminal is bent, so the letters are twisted into a new order
to conceal something is to hide it within, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: taken as written, letters for rearranging
a mag is a magazine

explanation.surface: An honest person turned criminal has hidden a document in a chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawer' looks like furniture, but it means something that draws, here pulling iron towards itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A U-shaped magnet attracts, or draws, iron and steel, so it is a drawer in the literal sense.

indicators.note: someone high is intoxicated, so the letters reel into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tall tree scores highly when set beside a may tree.
explanation.walkthrough: May is itself a tree, the hawthorn, which makes 'may tree' look like the definition; it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The sycamore is a large maple widespread in Britain, a common broad-leaved tree.

indicators.note: the letter is put inside the other word
in a down entry, coming up to the surface means reading from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female
the Nile is Africa's great river

explanation.surface: A dainty woman swimming in a river comes up for air.
explanation.definitionFit: Elfin describes something small and delicate in build, like an elf.

indicators.note: to cake something is to coat or encrust it, wrapping it round

blocks.note: a plain cake has no icing on it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Plain cakes don't stand out on the tea table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain cakes' reads as a noun phrase, but 'cakes' is a verb meaning coats, wrapping the plain one round 'not'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unnoticed escapes attention, which is what being inconspicuous means.

clue.text: Vainglorious concierge proving difficult, resident finally granted access

indicators.note: a difficult person won't behave, so the letters are thrown out of order
finally points to the closing letter of the word before it
being let in means going inside the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written, letters for rearranging
last letter of resident

explanation.surface: A conceited hotel concierge makes trouble before the resident is finally let in.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-centred person thinks only of themselves, much as a vain, boastful one does.

blocks.note: first meaning: a bad smell, as in British slang 'a hum'
second meaning: a style of dance music with a strong bass beat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hum' looks musical, but here it is the British slang for a stink; funk is an old word for a strong smell too.
explanation.definitionFit: Funk once meant a pungent smell, and it is also the name of a heavily rhythmic genre of popular music.

indicators.note: one word is placed inside the other

blocks.note: a stage is a step in a process
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: Third-class passengers are always kept in step.
explanation.definitionFit: Steerage was the cheapest passenger accommodation on a ship, the equivalent of third class.

blocks.note: first meaning: tiny, pronounced my-NEWT
second meaning: a written record or memo, pronounced MIN-it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a brief musical note; the two meanings are pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: Something minute is extremely small, and a minute is an official written record of a meeting.

indicators.note: something guzzled ends up swallowed inside, so the letters lie within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A werewolf drinks down a spirit as part of a ritual.
explanation.walkthrough: A lycanthrope is a werewolf; 'Spirit' tempts as a drink being guzzled, but it is a fairy.
explanation.definitionFit: A peri is a benevolent fairy-like being in Persian mythology, a kind of spirit.

clue.text: Maddening number surrounds the tailless burrower

indicators.note: without a tail, the word loses its last letter
to surround is to go all the way round something else

blocks.note: an earworm is a tune that sticks in the head and drives you mad
the word with its final letter cut off

explanation.surface: An irritating song goes on and on around some creature that has lost its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is a song here, not a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The earthworm spends its life tunnelling through soil, the archetypal burrowing animal.

blocks.note: a testing task is a hard one
a back is a defensive player in football

explanation.surface: A book that puts a footballer to the test.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'testing footballer' also reads as a tough defender, a hard back.
explanation.definitionFit: A hardback is a book bound in stiff covers, as opposed to a paperback.

clue.text: Radius, say, covering a district for military commander

indicators.note: a cover wraps round what it covers, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: the radius is a bone of the forearm; 'say' marks it as an example
taken as written
a part of town is a district

explanation.surface: A circle's radius is drawn over a district on a general's map.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radius' looks geometric; it is the forearm bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon Bonaparte was the French general and emperor, a famous military leader.

indicators.note: in a down entry, being above means coming first, which fixes the order

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'well!'
a niche is a recess in a wall

explanation.surface: A well sits higher than an alcove beside the cliff-top road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like a water source; it is the interjection.
explanation.definitionFit: A corniche is a road cut along the side of a cliff or coastline, often with sea views.

blocks.note: prim means proper and correct in manner
rose is a shade of pink

explanation.surface: A colour list runs from a proper pink to yellow.
explanation.walkthrough: With pink and yellow side by side, the clue looks like a list of colours; only 'yellow' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Primrose is a pale yellow shade, named after the colour of the spring flower.

clue.text: Nothing in Antigua and Barbuda, or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, last of all

indicators.note: the last of all the words means taking every word's final letter

blocks.note: last letter of this word
last letter of this word
last letter of this word
last letter of this word
an alternative route: the final letters of these words after 'or' spell the same thing

explanation.surface: A traveller finds nothing at all, whether in the Caribbean or the Balkans.
explanation.walkthrough: Either phrase works: 'in Bosnia and Herzegovina' also ends its words in the same four letters, so the setter offers both, joined by 'or'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nada is the Spanish word for nothing, borrowed into informal English.

clue.text: Hollow craft boarded by politician and yours truly

indicators.note: passengers who board a vessel go inside it

blocks.note: a craft is a skill or art
MP is a Member of Parliament
yours truly is the speaker, me

explanation.surface: A politician and I climb aboard an empty boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' suggests a boat, which suits 'boarded'; it is skill.
explanation.definitionFit: The armpit is the hollow under the shoulder where the arm joins the body.

clue.text: Old feudal leader unloads bullet finally from weapon

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it
unloading takes something out, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: last letter of bullet
a shotgun is a firearm

explanation.surface: An ancient warlord takes the last bullet out of his gun.
explanation.definitionFit: The shogun was the hereditary military ruler of feudal Japan.

clue.text: Roll with good twists for predatory reptile

indicators.note: something twisted round faces the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a roll is a list of names, as a rota is
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: An alligator rolls over, giving a good twist to catch its prey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll' suggests the alligator's death roll; it means a list.
explanation.definitionFit: Gator is the informal American name for the alligator, a predatory reptile.

clue.text: Suppose confronted by spreading of rat poison

indicators.note: being confronted by something means having it right in front, so that piece comes first
spreading things out scatters them, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, letters for rearranging
to opine is to suppose or state an opinion

explanation.surface: Someone imagines being faced with rat poison being spread around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rat poison' reads as one item, but 'rat' is the fodder and 'poison' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Atropine is a toxic alkaloid from deadly nightshade, a well-known poison.

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in place, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A crane, the wading bird, goes out hunting for shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre is mother-of-pearl, and dictionaries also give it as an old name for the pearl-bearing mollusc itself.

clue.text: Choice of left or right wing in parliament? Left!

indicators.note: the left wing of a word is its first letter
the right wing of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: the left-hand edge of this word
taken as written
the right-hand edge of this word

explanation.surface: An MP must choose between the left and right wings of parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: The political wings are the two ends of the word 'parliament', with 'or' kept as written between them.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship, port is the left-hand side when facing forward.

blocks.note: a con is a convict, so a felon's is a con's
piracy is the crime of robbery at sea

explanation.surface: A felon's crime is described as collusion between accomplices.
explanation.definitionFit: A conspiracy is a secret plot agreed between people, which is what collusion means.

indicators.note: something developing changes its shape, so the letters take a new form

blocks.note: taken as written, letters for rearranging
a gent is a gentleman, a man

explanation.surface: A mere infant grows into a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Infant' looks like a baby, but it is an adjective, as in an infant industry.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant industry is one just starting out, newly coming into being, which is emergent.

blocks.note: to secure something is to tie it fast
blood is red

explanation.surface: Securing supplies like those held in blood banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blood in banks' suggests a blood bank; 'banks' means rows, one above another.
explanation.definitionFit: Seats or shelves arranged in rising rows, as in a stadium, are tiered, set in banks.
